What this evidence can tell us

A genetic headline is only as strong as the study behind it. Six questions sort strong claims from weak ones in about a minute. This page gives you the questions, a table of study types, and two worked examples.

"A study found a link between gene X and ADHD" sounds like "gene X causes ADHD". It almost never means that. "Associated with" is a statistical statement about groups. It needs a sample size, a replication and an effect size before it means much.
What kind of study is it?
Has anyone else found the same thing?
Replication is the single best guard against false leads.
Children or adults? One ancestry group? Blood cells or brain?
What does the claim say it means?
"Associated with" is fine. "Causes" needs far more.

Begin with an associated locus, then evaluate fine-mapping, candidate variants, regulatory or coding consequences, potential effector genes and tissue-specific functions. Each step needs its own evidence. Linkage disequilibrium can leave several correlated candidates, and regulation may act over a distance. Proximity can be a clue but does not establish the causal gene by itself. These are complementary evidence types, not a mandatory sequence or a validated causal conclusion about one person.

One case treated as a rule

A 2009 meta-analytic review pooled earlier candidate-gene studies of childhood ADHD. It found significant associations for several genes, including DAT1, DRD4, DRD5, 5HTT, HTR1B and SNAP25. It also found significant heterogeneity for many of them, meaning the results differed from study to study

a real finding, at its time, from pre-chosen genes, with conflicting results between studies. It is a reason to keep looking, not a reason to call any of these "the ADHD gene". Later genome-wide studies use a different design
. Do not quote the 2009 list as if it were the modern GWAS result.
Worked example 2: a small blood-platelet study
A 2005 study measured binding to the vesicular monoamine transporter (

a.title: The protein that loads dopamine, serotonin and noradrenaline into storage vesicles

c: ) in blood platelets from 11 untreated boys and adolescents with ADHD and 14 controls. Binding capacity was 17% lower in the ADHD group, and lower binding went with higher symptom scores. The authors state that it is unclear whether platelet VMAT2 reflects the brain, and whether the difference is primary or a by-product
. Small, single study, children only, a peripheral proxy, and the authors' own caution. It justifies the question "is vesicle packaging involved in ADHD?" It does not answer it.
> A [study type] in [who, how many] found [what], which has [been / not yet been] replicated.
If you cannot fill all four blanks, the claim is not ready to be stated as fact.

A genetic overlay should state variant identity and evidence class, then examine the gene, tissue, mechanism and phenotype. Common statistical associations are different from a proven pathogenic rare variant, and rare-variant burden studies are not the same as a diagnosis from one unreviewed call. Connections between genes and pathways can generate research hypotheses. They do not justify arrows directly from a SNP label to a personal symptom or treatment recommendation.
